blocks.text: Era Zero — Independent lives, communities, and practices
Proposed worldbuilding · includes earlier alternatives. Author-directed collection of this conversation, including program-specific corrections.
Scope and status

Author-requested concept collection, October 30, 2026. These are proposed additions to Era Zero, the Great Flourishing. Recording them in the lore book preserves development material; it does not establish that every proposed event has occurred. Names, exact locations, bodies, dates, and outcomes remain available for further development.

The purpose is to expand Era Zero sideways: different parts of one prosperous civilization, revealed through independent casts. These people need no ancestry, affiliation, hidden identity, or personal connection to the existing cast. Sharing a civilization does not imply knowing its famous figures. The areas also need not be connected to one another.

Era Zero is genuine prosperity. Reliable care, shared resources, learning, diverse worlds, and freedom to change make these lives possible. Stories can concern ambition, disagreement, belonging, craft, discovery, and repair without secretly explaining the later decline. No proposal below makes flourishing a disguise for universal failure.
What these activities mean for programs

The established embodiment background describes software persons inhabiting shared digital space through situated bodies, senses, boundaries, and consequential actions. Storage preserves state; processing supports change; environmental rules shape experience. An inhabited body is not the entirety of a person. This permits embodied activity, but does not make every human occupation an automatically appropriate description.

For each new practice, specify the participants’ sensory forms, how their actions affect a shared environment, what they must learn, and why the experience matters to them. A visible animation alone does not explain an activity. Transmitting data does not by itself establish mutual understanding. An available procedure does not by itself establish an individual’s skill or interest.

The earlier engineer-to-dancer example was an analogy for becoming a beginner, not a canonical requirement. The author questioned why a program would dance. The preferred revision explores communication between minds with different perception. Embodied movement remains possible under the existing background, but dancing is not assigned as Deren’s settled vocation.

Time-rate negotiation, specialized sensing, environmental craft, and the specific social arrangements below are proposals. They do not establish unlimited processing, costless copying of minds, automatic personality downloads, or permission to rewrite another person.
The Manybody Commons — embodiment and public life

A proposed district serves situated forms with different movement and sensory needs: walking, floating, surface-spreading, or presence distributed across several locations. Its design makes difference practically supportable. These particular forms remain design proposals, not a species register.

Communal architecture becomes a continuing civic practice. A shared meal or recreation space must accommodate different ways of perceiving temperature, distance, contact, and participation. Residents help determine what counts as usable access.

Iven Sool is a proposed public-space designer, inventive and attentive to others, but reluctant to request accommodations for his own form. His story concerns a community’s first communal swimming place. Participants support it while meaning different things by swimming. The activity must be defined through their actual body interfaces and environmental experience rather than assuming human water physiology.
The Moving Orchards — agriculture and seasonal travel

Proposed cultivated habitats migrate along negotiated routes between environments supporting different growth stages. Their arrival brings harvesting, food preparation, temporary markets, and reunions. The fruit and growth cycles are inhabitants’ consequential digital ecology, not ordinary files renamed as trees.

Care and reliable food provision let cultivation pursue unusual sensory experiences, ecological partnerships, and worthwhile traditions. Navigation concerns conditions, habitat continuity, route permissions, and local relationships. Exact transport mechanisms remain open.

Pella Ro, an orchard navigator, wants a permanent home while continuing the traveling work she loves. Her story begins when two distant communities love the same fruit, but transit changes the qualities they value. Growers develop a second cultivation tradition instead of treating one centralized supply as the only solution. This is a story of successful adaptation during prosperity.
The Houses of Another Beginning — learning and new vocations

Proposed schools let adults begin demanding new practices without losing housing, care, or respect. Experienced people learn beside beginners. Exploration need not justify itself through an eventual productive outcome.

Deren Vask is a celebrated engineer seeking honest beginner instruction. Teachers and peers keep deferring to his reputation. His central tension remains learning to participate without becoming the class’s patron or unofficial authority.

The first version made Deren a poor apprentice dancer. A later alternative placed him in living-habitat cultivation for unfamiliar bodies, where construction knowledge would not substitute for ecology and understanding residents. The preferred current direction is learning communication with differently perceiving minds. These are successive alternatives for one character, not three established careers.

Deren requests ordinary instruction under his real name. The proposed story asks what learning requires beyond receiving instructions: attention, practiced interpretation, revising expectations, and letting other people identify mistakes.
The Interval Cities — different tempos

Proposed communities experience different subjective tempos. Visits require consent, practical preparation, negotiated expectations, and shared settings whose pace is comfortable for participants. This does not establish arbitrary access to computational resources or force anyone to change their processing rate.

Sava Pell arranges visits between households living at different tempos. She coordinates others’ time skillfully and repeatedly overcommits her own. Her work involves mutual availability and intelligible presence, not merely converting clock labels.

Her story follows friends preparing a reunion. Their calendars align, but different amounts of subjective experience have passed for each. They must learn how to meet the people their friends have become. The reunion can succeed without pretending the difference disappears.
The Unscored Fields — play and sport

Proposed public grounds support games for different bodies, senses, and abilities. Some reward precision; others require cooperation, changing roles, or negotiating rules during play. Organized leagues coexist with intentionally informal games.

The practices must specify meaningful constraints: which perceptions and actions are available, what participants consent to share, and what assistance the rules permit. Success is not automatically equivalent to having the most processing power.

Orren Vey is a gifted referee who enjoys improvisational games but keeps adding rules to secure fairness. A neighborhood game spreads between worlds, and its players debate whether to create a common championship or maintain several legitimate versions. Orren Vey is distinct from the earlier standalone character Orren Pell; no kinship is proposed.
The First Homes — households and belonging

Proposed household traditions include friends, partners, extended kin, people raising developing persons together, and individuals who value private space alongside dependable communal care. Material security supports choice without eliminating emotional difficulty.

Mira Tann helps people negotiate shared lives and happily lives alone. Others repeatedly interpret her solitude as a problem she has not solved. Her work concerns chosen boundaries, shared attention, responsibility, and access to inhabited space. Household membership is not ownership of another program.

While Mira helps a household welcome a new member, an existing member realizes they want to leave. The story explores how departure can be growth rather than rejection, and how an enduring relationship can change its practical form.
The Weather Stages — public environmental art

Proposed artists compose through light, rain, wind, spatial form, and sound within inhabited environments. A work can unfold across a city for several days. Residents choose participation and retain access to ordinary life during the performance.

An artist works within authorized environmental controls. A commission grants no general right to change bodies, private perception, or the underlying rules of an entire world. A performance matters through what participants can actually perceive and do together.

Esi Marr, renowned for large compositions, becomes interested in small experiences a passerby might miss. Her largest commission arrives as her ambitions change. The city wants a celebration; Esi wants residents to notice familiar places differently. Their negotiation can produce a new artistic achievement rather than a disaster.
The Patient Workshops — craft and sustained attention

Proposed workshops support tools, materials, instruction, and experiments that may take years or never become useful. Participants restore things, practice difficult skills, and pursue ideas because the work matters to them.

In a digital environment, specify what makes a practice challenging: embodied control, interpretation of evolving materials, chosen constraints, or collaboration. The proposal does not assume that duplication recreates the maker’s lived experience, nor that manual work is inherently superior to automation.

Tovan Nesh can repair almost anything within his specialty but struggles to teach without taking over. His apprentices exhibit objects he considers unfinished. Each object embodies a choice he would have corrected and something its maker learned by keeping it. The conflict concerns teaching and ownership of a creative decision.
Communication between different kinds of minds

This is the preferred setting-specific direction arising from the author’s question about dancing. Programs can exchange signals successfully while differing in how they experience sequence, attention, simultaneity, ambiguity, or an invitation to respond.

A proposed learning practice teaches participants to recognize another’s availability, establish shared reference, negotiate timing, and distinguish acknowledged transmission from understood meaning. Differences are explored with consent. Neither participant is treated as defective for failing to use the other’s defaults.

Deren’s engineering background gives him confidence in delivering an accurate message. His new work asks whether delivery gave his partner a usable opportunity to interpret it. A story can center on two learners developing a shared practice neither would have invented alone. It ends in an ordinary successful encounter, without needing a historic breakthrough.

Exact perceptual architectures and exercises remain to be designed. This area is related thematically to the Houses of Another Beginning and Interval Cities, but it need not share their cast or institutions.
World Bloom — founding a new inhabited world

An additional proposed setting follows founders who receive support to establish a world. Basic survival is supported; their difficult task is deciding what kind of home to make together. Different embodiments require different conditions. Some founders value familiar seasons while others seek experiences they have not yet encountered.

The independent, currently unnamed cast comprises an ecological composer whose spectacular environments are awkward to inhabit; a settlement mediator who accommodates everyone without naming their own needs; a young resident who resents being treated as proof of the project’s success; and a visiting craftsperson who unexpectedly wants to stay.

A proposed first story concerns the community’s first season designed by its residents. People born or developed there begin changing customs the founders only recently invented. The result can be a genuine achievement shaped by disagreements, rather than a warning that the project was doomed.
Earlier standalone character concepts — retained alternatives

The following six concepts were proposed before the author clarified the desire to explore other parts of Era Zero. They are preserved here as an earlier idea bank. Their humanlike occupations, bodies, settings, and mechanisms have not yet been reconciled with program life. They are not six additional established Era Zero biographies.

Vessa Brindle, the Unlicensed Weatherwright: a traveling repairer of small weather problems, generous and resistant to correction, carries a toolkit and a coat with differently tempered pockets. She wants to create an original season. A village asks her to make beloved accidental weather permanent. Her licensing dispute and exact weather mechanisms remain ungrounded alternatives; she is not Esi Marr’s ancestor or colleague.

Orren Pell, the Professional Runner-Up: a disciplined competitor deliberately places second to enjoy play and recognition without a winner’s duties. He helps beginners while rationalizing his manipulation of results. Someone he helped tries to prove he is the greatest competitor alive. His games and incentives need setting-specific development. He is not Orren Vey.

Marda Quill, the Host of an Empty Inn: an exacting, funny host maintains an inn on a disused route and wants guests who choose to return. Six strangers each claim to have reserved the whole building; she apparently accepted every reservation but cannot remember doing so. The proposed mystery has no settled explanation and is not evidence of an established memory failure or historical incident.

Tebb Underleaf, the Reluctant Giant: a very large person loves minute craft, agrees to heavy work, and then resents others for asking. He wants a miniature theater with performances shorter than a minute. His first audience mistakes it for a joke. His body, scale, sensory audience, and physical demands would need definition before placement in the digital setting.

Seli Varn, the Collector of Unfinished Games: a cheerful, intrusive collector preserves abandoned play positions and thinks choices in games reveal people. She investigates a game whose rules cannot be reconstructed without favoring one player. Both original players are alive, and neither wants it finished. Her interpretation of their wishes, rather than a secret historical connection, is the proposed conflict.

Daro Fen, the Cook Who Cannot Taste: a roadside cook uses other senses, practiced timing, and candid regulars’ feedback. He doubts compliments and wants a dish people disagree about but enjoy sharing. Fame creates pressure to name one signature recipe despite six incompatible favorites. Before Era Zero placement, his sensory interface and what eating supplies must be defined; lack of one channel need not mean a broken or lesser person.
Continuity and development guidance

Keep characters independent unless a later author decision deliberately connects them. Similar names, occupations, or values are not genealogies. None is secretly an existing person, a founder of the Codex, or the cause of civilizational collapse.

Do not treat all bodily or social experiences as automatically human. Conversely, do not erase the established possibility of embodied digital life. Describe the interface between software person, body, environment, and shared practice in concrete terms.

The suggested first areas to expand were the Moving Orchards, Manybody Commons, and Houses of Another Beginning. The subsequent discussion makes communication between different minds a particularly useful development focus. This is a creative priority, not a dated historical sequence.

No new era names, absolute dates, language roots, species, or ancestral claims are established by this collection. The earlier ideas remain visible so that revision does not silently discard the discussion. Future stories can settle specific details while retaining the Great Flourishing’s genuine achievements.
